On initialisation, it delegates connection setup to the parent class and additionally creates a `ProfilesRepository` instance stored as `self._profiles_repo`, which is used internally to resolve comment author profiles [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository::__init__]]. It is not a Pydantic model [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]].

The private helper `_get_comment_from_db_record` constructs a `Comment` domain object from a raw database row, reading `id`, `body`, `created_at`, and `updated_at` directly from that row, then asynchronously resolving the author's profile via `self._profiles_repo.get_profile_by_username` so that follow relationships are correctly reflected from the requesting user's perspective [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository::_get_comment_from_db_record]].

New comments are persisted by `create_comment_for_article`, which writes the row to the database and immediately hydrates it into a full `Comment` domain object through `_get_comment_from_db_record`, making the entire operation fully asynchronous [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository::create_comment_for_article]]. A single comment can be retrieved by its numeric ID and parent article slug using `get_comment_by_id`, which raises `EntityDoesNotExist` when no matching row is found [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository::get_comment_by_id]]. All comments belonging to an article can be fetched at once through `get_comments_for_article`, which queries by slug and maps each returned row to a domain object via the same helper [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository::get_comments_for_article]]. Finally, `delete_comment` permanently removes a comment from the database given a `Comment` object as its target [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository::delete_comment]].

`ProfilesRepository` is a database repository class responsible for managing user profile data and follower relationships, defined in [`target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py`](target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py) [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. It is not a Pydantic model. It inherits directly from `BaseRepository` [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]], extending the base connection-management infrastructure for profile-specific operations [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]].

During initialisation, the constructor delegates connection setup to the parent class via `super().__init__(conn)` and then creates an internal `UsersRepository` instance bound to the same connection, storing it as `self._users_repo` so that profile operations can cross-reference user data without opening a separate connection [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository::__init__]].

The class exposes four public async methods. `get_profile_by_username` looks up a user record through `self._users_repo` and assembles a `Profile` object populated with the user's `username`, `bio`, and `image`; when an optional `requested_user` argument is supplied it also resolves the `following` field by delegating to `is_user_following_for_another_user` [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository::get_profile_by_username]]. `is_user_following_for_another_user` queries the database with the two users' usernames and returns the `"is_following"` boolean extracted directly from the query result [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository::is_user_following_for_another_user]]. `add_user_into_followers` persists a follow relationship inside an atomic transaction by calling `queries.subscribe_user_to_another` with the follower's and the target's usernames; both parameters are keyword-only and typed as `UserLike` [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository::add_user_into_followers]]. Finally, `remove_user_from_followers` mirrors that operation in reverse, executing `queries.unsubscribe_user_from_another` inside a transaction to atomically delete the follow record between the two users [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository::remove_user_from_followers]].

`TagsRepository` is a database repository class that inherits from `BaseRepository` and is responsible for managing tag records in the database [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]] [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]]. It is not a Pydantic model [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]]. The class defines two asynchronous methods [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]].

The first, `create_tags_that_dont_exist`, accepts a sequence of tag strings and persists any that do not yet exist by delegating to `queries.create_new_tags`, passing the repository's active connection alongside the tags mapped into a list of `{"tag": tag}` dicts [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository::create_tags_that_dont_exist]]. It returns nothing [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository::create_tags_that_dont_exist]].

The second, `get_all_tags`, queries the database for all tags by calling `queries.get_all_tags` with the repository's active connection [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository::get_all_tags]]. It returns a flat `List[str]` by extracting the first element from each row in the result set [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository::get_all_tags]].

`UsersRepository` is a database repository class responsible for all persistence operations on user records, including creation, lookup, and update [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]]. It inherits from `BaseRepository`, which provides the underlying database connection management [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]]. It is not a Pydantic model.

The `create_user` method builds a new `UserInDB` instance from the supplied username and email, salts and hashes the password via `change_password`, then inserts the record inside an explicit transaction using `queries.create_new_user` [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository::create_user]]. The resulting database row is merged back onto the in-memory model so that any database-generated values such as the assigned `id` are reflected in the returned object [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository::create_user]].

The `get_user_by_email` method queries the database for a single row matching the given email address, hydrates it into a `UserInDB` model on success, and raises `EntityDoesNotExist` if no matching row is found [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository::get_user_by_email]]. Similarly, `get_user_by_username` delegates to `queries.get_user_by_username` using the repository's active connection, returns a `UserInDB` when a row is found, and raises `EntityDoesNotExist` when the username is absent [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository::get_user_by_username]].

The `update_user` method first fetches the current persisted state via `get_user_by_username`, then selectively applies only those optional fields — `username`, `email`, `bio`, `image` — for which a non-falsy value was provided, leaving the rest unchanged [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository::update_user]]. When a new password is supplied, `change_password` is invoked to refresh the salt and hashed password before any write occurs [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository::update_user]]. All writes are executed inside a database transaction, after which the fully updated `UserInDB` record is returned to the caller [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository::update_user]].

This module serves as the application entry point for the FastAPI service, responsible for assembling and exposing the fully configured application instance [[target/app/main.py]]. It defines a single factory function, `get_application`, and immediately invokes it at module level to produce the `app` object that ASGI servers consume [[target/app/main.py]].

The `get_application` function begins by retrieving application settings via `get_app_settings` and configuring logging through those settings [[target/app/main.py::get_application]]. It then constructs a `FastAPI` instance using keyword arguments sourced directly from the settings object [[target/app/main.py::get_application]]. `CORSMiddleware` is attached to the application to permit all methods and headers from the configured allowed hosts, with credentials enabled [[target/app/main.py::get_application]]. Lifecycle management is wired in by registering startup and shutdown handlers produced by `create_start_app_handler` and `create_stop_app_handler` respectively [[target/app/main.py::get_application]]. Application-level error handling is established by mapping `HTTPException` to `http_error_handler` and `RequestValidationError` to `http422_error_handler` [[target/app/main.py::get_application]]. Finally, the API router is mounted under the URL prefix defined in settings, and the fully configured `FastAPI` instance is returned to the call site [[target/app/main.py::get_application]].

`DateTimeModelMixin` is a Pydantic model that mixes timestamp-tracking behaviour into other models [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]]. It inherits from `BaseModel` [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]] and declares two fields: `created_at` and `updated_at`, both typed as `datetime.datetime` and defaulting to `None` [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]]. A `pre` validator named `default_datetime` is attached to both fields; it returns the supplied value unchanged when it is truthy, and falls back to the current datetime via `datetime.datetime.now()` when the value is absent or falsy [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin::default_datetime]]. This ensures that both timestamps are always populated with a meaningful value at the time of model instantiation even if the caller omits them [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin::default_datetime]].

The file `target/app/models/domain/articles.py` defines the core domain model for articles within the application [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py]]. Its sole export is the `Article` class, a Pydantic model that represents a fully realised published article [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py::Article]].

`Article` composes three base classes — `IDModelMixin`, `DateTimeModelMixin`, and `RWModel` — to inherit identity, timestamp, and serialisation behaviour without duplicating that logic [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py::Article]]. Through `IDModelMixin` it receives an `id_` integer field aliased to the JSON key `"id"`, and through `DateTimeModelMixin` it gains `created_at` and `updated_at` datetime fields that track the article's lifecycle [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py::Article]].

On top of those inherited fields, `Article` declares eight fields of its own [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py::Article]]. The `slug` and `title` strings carry the URL-friendly identifier and human-readable headline, while `description` and `body` hold the short summary and full article content respectively [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py::Article]]. A `tags` field typed as `List[str]` associates the article with zero or more topic labels, and an `author` field typed as `Profile` links the article directly to the user who wrote it [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py::Article]]. Rounding out the model, `favorited` is a boolean indicating whether the article has been favourited by the requesting user, and `favorites_count` is an integer recording the total number of times it has been favourited across all users [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py::Article]].

The module [`target/app/models/domain/comments.py`](target/app/models/domain/comments.py) defines the domain-layer representation of a comment, importing the shared mixins and base model it needs from elsewhere in the application [[target/app/models/domain/comments.py]]. Its sole export is the `Comment` model, a Pydantic class that composes identity, timestamps, and comment-specific data into a single cohesive type [[target/app/models/domain/comments.py::Comment]].

`Comment` inherits from `IDModelMixin`, `DateTimeModelMixin`, and `RWModel`, pulling in all shared structure from those bases rather than redefining it [[target/app/models/domain/comments.py::Comment]]. From `IDModelMixin` it gains an `id_` field typed as `int`, serialised under the JSON key `"id"`, which uniquely identifies each comment [[target/app/models/domain/comments.py::Comment]]. From `DateTimeModelMixin` it inherits `created_at` and `updated_at`, both `datetime.datetime` fields that track when the comment was first created and when it was last changed [[target/app/models/domain/comments.py::Comment]]. The `RWModel` base supplies the shared Pydantic configuration applied consistently across domain models in this application [[target/app/models/domain/comments.py::Comment]].

On top of those inherited fields, `Comment` adds two fields of its own: `body`, a `str` that holds the comment's text content, and `author`, a `Profile` instance that records who wrote the comment [[target/app/models/domain/comments.py::Comment]]. Together, these pieces give the type everything needed to represent a fully-formed comment — its identity, its content, its authorship, and its lifecycle timestamps — in a single validated structure [[target/app/models/domain/comments.py::Comment]].

The module [`target/app/models/domain/profiles.py`](target/app/models/domain/profiles.py) defines the domain-layer representation of a user profile [[target/app/models/domain/profiles.py]]. It imports `Optional` from the standard library and `RWModel` from the project's shared domain model base, which together support the single class it exposes [[target/app/models/domain/profiles.py]].

That class, `Profile`, is a Pydantic model that captures the information associated with a user profile [[target/app/models/domain/profiles.py::Profile]]. It inherits from `RWModel`, picking up the shared serialisation behaviour that base class provides to all domain models [[target/app/models/domain/profiles.py::Profile]]. The class declares four fields: `username`, a required `str` that uniquely identifies the profile; `bio`, a `str` that defaults to an empty string; `image`, an `Optional[str]` that defaults to `None` to allow a profile to exist without a photo; and `following`, a `bool` that defaults to `False` to indicate whether the currently authenticated user follows this profile [[target/app/models/domain/profiles.py::Profile]].

This module defines the shared serialisation infrastructure for all domain models in the project [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py]]. It imports `datetime` from the standard library alongside Pydantic's `BaseConfig` and `BaseModel`, and builds three closely related components on top of those primitives [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py]].

The first is `convert_field_to_camel_case`, a utility function that transforms a snake\_case field name into camelCase by splitting on underscores, leaving the first word as-is, and capitalising the initial letter of every subsequent word before rejoining them [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::convert_field_to_camel_case]]. The second is `convert_datetime_to_realworld`, which accepts a `datetime.datetime` object, coerces its timezone info to UTC, renders it as an ISO 8601 string, and then replaces the trailing `+00:00` offset with a `Z` suffix to produce the compact timestamp format expected by the API [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::convert_datetime_to_realworld]].

Both functions feed directly into `RWModel`, the base Pydantic model that every domain model in the codebase inherits from [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::RWModel]]. `RWModel` extends `BaseModel` and carries an inner `Config` class derived from `BaseConfig` that wires the two functions into the model layer [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::RWModel]]. The `alias_generator` is set to `convert_field_to_camel_case`, so every snake\_case Python field automatically gains a camelCase alias for JSON serialisation without any per-field annotation [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py]]. The `json_encoders` mapping delegates `datetime.datetime` serialisation to `convert_datetime_to_realworld`, ensuring consistent UTC timestamps whenever a model is dumped to JSON [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py]]. Finally, `allow_population_by_field_name = True` allows model instances to be constructed using either the Python name or the generated camelCase alias, preventing breakage on the input side [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py]]. `RWModel` itself declares no fields; its sole purpose is to propagate these three configuration choices uniformly to every subclass [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::RWModel]].

`UserInDB` is a Pydantic model that represents a user record as it is stored in the database [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. It inherits from three base classes: `IDModelMixin`, `DateTimeModelMixin`, and `User` [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. From `IDModelMixin` it gains an `id_` field of type `int`, declared with `Field(0, alias="id")` so that it maps to the JSON key `"id"` [[target/app/models/common.py::IDModelMixin]]. From `DateTimeModelMixin` it gains `created_at` and `updated_at` fields, both typed as `datetime.datetime` and defaulting to `None` [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]]. From `User` it inherits `username` and `email` (both `str`), `bio` (a `str` defaulting to `""`), and `image` (an `Optional[str]` defaulting to `None`) [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::User]]. On top of those inherited fields, `UserInDB` adds two fields of its own: `salt` and `hashed_password`, both typed as `str` and defaulting to `""` [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]].

The class exposes two methods for managing credentials. `change_password` updates the instance in place by generating a fresh salt via `security.generate_salt`, storing it in `self.salt`, then hashing the concatenation of that salt and the supplied plain-text password via `security.get_password_hash` and storing the result in `self.hashed_password`; the method returns nothing [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB::change_password]]. `check_password` verifies a supplied plain-text password by concatenating `self.salt` with it and delegating to `security.verify_password` together with `self.hashed_password`, returning `True` on a match and `False` otherwise [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB::check_password]].

[`target/app/models/schemas/articles.py`](target/app/models/schemas/articles.py) is the articles schema module, responsible for defining the Pydantic models that shape article data as it moves in and out of the API [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py]]. It also establishes two module-level pagination constants — `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_LIMIT` (20) and `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_OFFSET` (0) — that are reused by the filter model [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py]].

The module's schemas divide naturally into request shapes, response shapes, and a query-filter shape. On the request side, `ArticleInCreate` captures the data needed to create a new article: the required `title`, `description`, and `body` strings, plus an optional `tags` list exposed under the alias `"tagList"` [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInCreate]]. `ArticleInUpdate` handles partial edits by making all three text fields — `title`, `description`, and `body` — `Optional[str]` defaulting to `None`, so a caller can supply any combination without being forced to repeat unchanged values [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInUpdate]].

On the response side, `ArticleForResponse` is the central building block: it inherits the full set of article domain fields from `Article` and adds its own `tags` field (aliased `"tagList"`), producing the complete shape used whenever a single article is serialised for the API [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleForResponse]]. `ArticleInResponse` wraps that shape in a single `article` field of type `ArticleForResponse`, forming the envelope returned by single-article endpoints [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInResponse]]. For list endpoints, `ListOfArticlesInResponse` holds an `articles` field typed as `List[ArticleForResponse]` together with a required `articles_count` integer, covering both the result set and its total count in one response object [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ListOfArticlesInResponse]].

`ArticlesFilters` stands apart from the request/response pair as a query-parameter model: it inherits directly from `BaseModel` rather than `RWSchema` and bundles the three optional string filters `tag`, `author`, and `favorited` with `limit` and `offset` pagination fields, the latter two constrained by the module-level defaults and validated lower bounds [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticlesFilters]]. All five schemas that participate in API serialisation — `ArticleForResponse`, `ArticleInCreate`, `ArticleInResponse`, `ArticleInUpdate`, and `ListOfArticlesInResponse` — inherit from `RWSchema`, which provides the shared camelCase aliasing behaviour throughout the module [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleForResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInCreate]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInUpdate]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ListOfArticlesInResponse]].

This module defines the Pydantic request and response schemas for comment-related API operations [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py]]. It imports `Comment` from the domain layer and `RWSchema` as the shared base, then builds three schema classes on top of them [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py]].

`CommentInCreate` handles the input side: it validates the payload when a new comment is submitted, exposing a single `body` field of type `str` that holds the comment text [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInCreate]]. On the output side, `CommentInResponse` wraps a single `Comment` domain object in a `comment` field, forming the envelope returned by the API for a single-comment response [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInResponse]]. When multiple comments must be returned, `ListOfCommentsInResponse` takes over, holding a `List[Comment]` under a `comments` field [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::ListOfCommentsInResponse]]. All three classes inherit from `RWSchema`, which supplies the shared serialisation configuration common to every request and response schema in the application [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInCreate]] [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::ListOfCommentsInResponse]].

This module defines the Pydantic schemas used to represent the structured data carried inside JSON Web Tokens [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py]]. It imports `datetime` from the standard library and `BaseModel` from Pydantic, which both schema classes build upon [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py]].

`JWTMeta` is a Pydantic model that captures the standard metadata fields of a JWT [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTMeta]]. It declares two required fields: `exp`, typed as `datetime`, which holds the token's expiration time, and `sub`, typed as `str`, which carries the subject of the token — typically a user identifier [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTMeta]]. Because neither field has a default value, both must be supplied whenever an instance is constructed [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTMeta]].

`JWTUser` is a companion Pydantic model that represents the user identity extracted from a JWT [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTUser]]. It holds a single field, `username`, typed as `str`, carrying just enough information to identify the authenticated subject once a token has been decoded [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTUser]].

Together, the two models separate concerns cleanly: `JWTMeta` covers the token-level properties such as expiry and subject, while `JWTUser` carries the application-level identity derived from that token [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTMeta]] [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTUser]].

This module defines the schema layer for profile-related API responses [[target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py]]. It imports Pydantic's `BaseModel` and the `Profile` domain model, then uses them to build a single response wrapper [[target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py]]. The only class it defines is `ProfileInResponse`, a Pydantic model that acts as the response envelope for a profile resource [[target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py::ProfileInResponse]]. It inherits directly from `BaseModel` and declares one field, `profile`, typed as `Profile`, ensuring the returned JSON always wraps the profile object under a `profile` key [[target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py::ProfileInResponse]]. Field validation and serialisation are handled automatically by Pydantic, requiring no additional boilerplate in this file [[target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py::ProfileInResponse]].

This module serves as the schema foundation layer for ORM-compatible Pydantic models in the application [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py]]. It imports `RWModel` from the domain layer and defines a single class, `RWSchema`, which extends it [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]]. The sole purpose of `RWSchema` is to enable `orm_mode = True` through a nested `Config` class that inherits from `RWModel.Config`, allowing Pydantic to populate model instances directly from ORM objects such as database rows, rather than only from plain dictionaries [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]]. No new fields are introduced at this level; the full field set is inherited entirely from `RWModel` [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]]. Any schema class in the application that needs to be constructed from database query results should inherit from `RWSchema` rather than `RWModel` directly, making this module the thin but essential bridge between the domain model layer and persistence-aware schema classes [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]].

The [`tags.py`](target/app/models/schemas/tags.py) module defines the Pydantic schema used to represent a collection of tags [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py]]. It imports `List` from the standard `typing` module and `BaseModel` from Pydantic, which together form the basis of its single data model [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py]].

The only class defined in this module is [`TagsInList`](target/app/models/schemas/tags.py::TagsInList), a Pydantic model that inherits directly from `BaseModel` [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py::TagsInList]]. It declares one field, `tags`, typed as `List[str]`, which holds a list of tag name strings [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py::TagsInList]]. The model serves as a structured container for returning or transmitting a set of tags as a validated payload [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py::TagsInList]].

This module defines the complete set of request and response schemas for user-related API operations, building on Pydantic for validation and the project's shared `RWSchema` base class [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py]].

The login flow begins with `UserInLogin`, which captures the two credentials a user submits at sign-in: a validated `email` field typed as `EmailStr` and a plain `password` string, both inherited by schemas further up the hierarchy [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInLogin]]. Registration extends that foundation through `UserInCreate`, which inherits `email` and `password` from `UserInLogin` and adds the required `username` field, making it the complete three-field schema needed to create a new account [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInCreate]].

On the response side, `UserWithToken` extends the domain `User` class, inheriting its `username`, `email`, `bio`, and `image` fields and adding a single required `token` string so that authenticated responses can carry both profile data and the session token in one object [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserWithToken]]. That combined representation is then wrapped by `UserInResponse`, whose sole field is a `user` typed as `UserWithToken`; this outer envelope is what the API actually returns to callers after a successful login or registration [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInResponse]].

Account updates are handled separately by `UserInUpdate`, which inherits directly from `BaseModel` rather than `RWSchema` and declares all five editable fields — `username`, `email`, `password`, `bio`, and `image` — as optional with `None` defaults [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInUpdate]]. Because every field is optional, a caller may send any subset of changes, and an empty payload remains valid while only explicitly supplied fields carry update intent [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInUpdate]].

The `resources` package acts as the home for shared, application-wide assets that any other part of the codebase can import [[target/app/resources]]. Its [`__init__.py`](target/app/resources/__init__.py) marks the directory as a Python package and serves as the entry point for any shared resource definitions or re-exports used across the application [[target/app/resources/__init__.py]].

The substantive work of the package lives in [`strings.py`](target/app/resources/strings.py), which is a central registry of human-readable API error and status message strings [[target/app/resources/strings.py]]. Rather than scattering raw string literals throughout the codebase, every error or status message is declared once as a named module-level constant, so any code path that needs to surface a message to a client can import it by name and stay consistent with every other caller [[target/app/resources/strings.py]].

The constants are organised around several concern areas. User-related errors cover a missing user, duplicate username or email at registration, and incorrect login credentials [[target/app/resources/strings.py]]. Article-related errors address the cases where an article does not exist, already exists, has already been favorited, is not currently favorited, or where the requesting user is not its author [[target/app/resources/strings.py]]. Follow and subscription errors describe attempts to follow or unfollow oneself, following a user that is already followed, and unfollowing a user that is not currently followed [[target/app/resources/strings.py]]. Authentication errors handle an unsupported authorization prefix, a payload that cannot be validated, and a general authentication-required condition [[target/app/resources/strings.py]]. A comment error constant covers the case where a requested comment does not exist [[target/app/resources/strings.py]].

Taken together, the two files give the `resources` package a single, well-defined responsibility: centralise every piece of user-facing text so that error messages remain consistent and can be updated in one location rather than hunted across the entire application [[target/app/resources/strings.py]] [[target/app/resources/__init__.py]].

This module provides a small set of article-related service utilities that sit between the API layer and the database and domain models [[target/app/services/articles.py]]. It imports from the repository, domain models, and error types to support three focused helper functions [[target/app/services/articles.py]].

The `check_article_exists` function accepts an `ArticlesRepository` and a slug string, delegating the lookup to `articles_repo.get_article_by_slug` and returning `True` if the article is found or `False` if an `EntityDoesNotExist` exception is raised [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_article_exists]]. This makes it a safe, boolean-returning guard that callers can use without handling database exceptions themselves [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_article_exists]].

The `check_user_can_modify_article` function complements the existence check by enforcing ownership: it compares the article's author username against the requesting user's username and returns `True` only when they match [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_user_can_modify_article]]. Together, these two functions form a natural pair — first confirming an article exists, then confirming the acting user is allowed to change it [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_article_exists]] [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_user_can_modify_article]].

Finally, `get_slug_for_article` handles the transformation of a raw article title into a URL-friendly slug by delegating directly to the `slugify` library [[target/app/services/articles.py::get_slug_for_article]], keeping slug generation consistent and centralised across any code that needs to derive a slug from a title [[target/app/services/articles.py::get_slug_for_article]].

This module provides authentication-related helper utilities for checking whether user credentials are already registered in the system [[target/app/services/authentication.py]]. It imports `EntityDoesNotExist` from the database errors layer and relies on `UsersRepository` to perform its lookups [[target/app/services/authentication.py]].

The `check_email_is_taken` function accepts a `UsersRepository` and an email string, queries the repository for a matching user, and returns `True` if one is found or `False` if `EntityDoesNotExist` is raised [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_email_is_taken]]. Similarly, `check_username_is_taken` calls `repo.get_user_by_username` and returns `True` when the username is already registered, or `False` when `EntityDoesNotExist` is raised, indicating the username is available [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken]]. Both functions share the same pattern of translating a repository-level `EntityDoesNotExist` exception into a plain boolean result, giving callers a clean availability check without needing to handle exceptions directly [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_email_is_taken]] [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken]].

This module provides authorization logic for comment operations, importing the `Comment` and `User` domain models to support its work [[target/app/services/comments.py]]. It exposes a single function, `check_user_can_modify_comment`, which accepts a `Comment` and a `User` and returns `True` only when the comment's author username matches the given user's username, enforcing the rule that a user may only modify their own comments [[target/app/services/comments.py::check_user_can_modify_comment]].

This module centralises all JWT-related logic for the application, providing token creation and decoding utilities built on the `HS256` algorithm with a fixed one-week expiry window [[target/app/services/jwt.py]].

`create_jwt_token` is the low-level building block: it takes an arbitrary payload dictionary, computes an expiry timestamp by adding the supplied `expires_delta` to the current UTC time, merges in a `JWTMeta` record carrying that expiry and the module-level `JWT_SUBJECT` constant, and returns the resulting signed JWT string [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_jwt_token]].

`create_access_token_for_user` sits one level above it, accepting a `User` object and a `secret_key`, extracting the username into a `JWTUser` struct, and delegating to `create_jwt_token` with the serialised payload and an expiry window derived from `ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES` [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_access_token_for_user]]. It returns the final signed JWT string to the caller [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_access_token_for_user]].

`get_username_from_token` handles the reverse direction: it decodes a JWT string with the provided `secret_key`, wraps the payload in a `JWTUser` model, and returns the `username` field [[target/app/services/jwt.py::get_username_from_token]]. Decode failures raise `ValueError("unable to decode JWT token")`, and payload validation failures raise `ValueError("malformed payload in token")`, ensuring callers receive a clear signal for either class of problem [[target/app/services/jwt.py::get_username_from_token]].

This module provides password-security utilities for the application, centralising all cryptographic operations in one place [[target/app/services/security.py]]. It initialises a `passlib` `CryptContext` configured to use the bcrypt hashing scheme, which the hashing and verification functions share [[target/app/services/security.py]].

`generate_salt` produces a fresh random cryptographic salt on each call by invoking `bcrypt.gensalt()` and decoding the raw bytes into a UTF-8 string before returning it [[target/app/services/security.py::generate_salt]]. `get_password_hash` accepts a plain-text password and returns a bcrypt hash of it by delegating to the shared `pwd_context.hash` [[target/app/services/security.py::get_password_hash]]. `verify_password` takes a plain-text password alongside its stored hash, calls `pwd_context.verify` to compare them, and returns `True` on a match or `False` otherwise [[target/app/services/security.py::verify_password]]. Together, `get_password_hash` and `verify_password` form a complementary pair for storing and later authenticating user credentials [[target/app/services/security.py::get_password_hash]] [[target/app/services/security.py::verify_password]].

This module provides the complete authentication dependency layer for the FastAPI application, handling JWT Bearer token extraction, validation, and user resolution for both required and optional authentication scenarios [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py]].

The foundation is `RWAPIKeyHeader`, a subclass of FastAPI's `APIKeyHeader` that overrides `__call__` to catch any `StarletteHTTPException` raised by the parent and re-raise it as an application-level `HTTPException` with the detail message set to `strings.AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED`, ensuring a consistent error shape across the API [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader]].

Token extraction is handled by two complementary functions. `_get_authorization_header` splits the raw header value on a space, verifies the prefix matches the configured `jwt_token_prefix`, and returns the bare token string, raising an HTTP 403 exception if either check fails [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]]. `_get_authorization_header_optional` wraps that logic: when a header is present it delegates to `_get_authorization_header`, and when none is supplied it returns an empty string instead of raising an error, relying on `RWAPIKeyHeader` configured with `auto_error=False` to make the header absence non-fatal [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]]. The factory function `_get_authorization_header_retriever` selects between these two by returning `_get_authorization_header` when `required=True` or `_get_authorization_header_optional` when `required=False` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]].

User resolution follows the same required/optional pattern. `_get_current_user` decodes the JWT using the app's secret key to extract a username, raises HTTP 403 if the payload is malformed, then fetches the matching `User` from `UsersRepository`, raising a second HTTP 403 if no such user exists [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]]. `_get_current_user_optional` provides the relaxed variant: it uses `_get_authorization_header_retriever` with `required=False`, and when no token is present it returns `None` rather than raising, delegating to `_get_current_user` only when a token is actually provided [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]].

The public entry point for route authors is `get_current_user_authorizer`, a factory that returns `_get_current_user` when `required=True` (the default) or `_get_current_user_optional` when `required=False`, yielding a `Callable` ready to be declared as a FastAPI dependency that enforces or relaxes authentication depending on the needs of each route [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]].

The `errors` package serves as the centralised error-handling layer for the FastAPI application's API tier, grouping the modules responsible for shaping all error responses into a consistent `{"errors": [...]}` envelope [[target/app/api/errors]]. The directory is declared as a Python package by an empty initialiser that provides no definitions of its own but establishes the `app.api.errors` import namespace for the sibling modules it contains [[target/app/api/errors/__init__.py]].

Two handler modules live inside the package, each targeting a distinct error category. The first, [`http_error.py`](target/app/api/errors/http_error.py), handles general HTTP exceptions by exposing `http_error_handler`, which receives a request and an `HTTPException`, wraps the exception's detail in the shared `{"errors": [...]}` list structure, and returns a `JSONResponse` preserving the original status code [[target/app/api/errors/http_error.py::http_error_handler]]. The second, [`validation_error.py`](target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py), addresses input-validation failures on two fronts: at import time it patches the OpenAPI schema definition so that the generated documentation advertises the same `{"errors": ...}` envelope shape, and at runtime its `http422_error_handler` function extracts structured validation details via `exc.errors()` and returns them in that same envelope with HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py]] [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py::http422_error_handler]]. Together the two modules ensure that both the live API responses and the static OpenAPI documentation remain consistent in structure for every error the application can surface [[target/app/api/errors/http_error.py]] [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py]].

The `articles` package forms a self-contained routing layer that delivers the complete articles API to the rest of the application [[target/app/api/routes/articles]]. Its [`__init__.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/__init__.py) marks the directory as an importable Python package so that other parts of the codebase can reference its contents [[target/app/api/routes/articles/__init__.py]].

The package is divided across two functional modules that are stitched together by a single aggregator. [`api.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/api.py) acts as that aggregator: it imports the routers from both sibling modules, mounts each under the `/articles` prefix, and exposes one unified `router` object for registration elsewhere in the application [[target/app/api/routes/articles/api.py]].

[`articles_resource.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py) covers the core CRUD lifecycle of an article [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py]]. `list_articles` handles `GET /api/articles` with optional authentication, filtering by tag, author, or favourited state, and returns a paginated `ListOfArticlesInResponse` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]]. `create_new_article` handles `POST /api/articles`, derives a URL-safe slug from the title, and rejects the request with HTTP 400 if that slug already exists [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::create_new_article]]. `retrieve_article_by_slug` handles `GET /api/articles/{slug}` and returns the resolved article wrapped in an `ArticleInResponse` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]]. `update_article_by_slug` handles `PUT /api/articles/{slug}` and enforces write-access via `check_article_modification_permissions` before applying changes and re-deriving the slug when a new title is supplied [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]]. `delete_article_by_slug` handles `DELETE /api/articles/{slug}`, applies the same permission guard, and responds with HTTP 204 No Content after permanent removal [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::delete_article_by_slug]].

[`articles_common.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py) extends that surface with feed and favouriting behaviour [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py]]. `get_articles_for_user_feed` handles `GET /api/articles/feed`, returning a paginated and personalised article feed for the authenticated caller using `limit` and `offset` parameters [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::get_articles_for_user_feed]]. `mark_article_as_favorite` handles `POST /api/articles/{slug}/favorite`, persisting the favouriting relationship and returning the updated article; it raises HTTP 400 if the article is already favourited [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]]. `remove_article_from_favorites` mirrors that logic on `DELETE /api/articles/{slug}/favorite`, decrementing `favorites_count` and patching `favorited` to `False`, or raising HTTP 400 if the article was not previously favourited [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::remove_article_from_favorites]]. All three handlers share a consistent dependency-injection pattern, resolving the acting user via `get_current_user_authorizer` and the data layer via `get_repository` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::get_articles_for_user_feed]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::remove_article_from_favorites]].

[`target/app/core/logging.py`](target/app/core/logging.py) is a small bridging module whose sole purpose is to connect Python's built-in `logging` infrastructure to the Loguru library [[target/app/core/logging.py]]. It imports the standard `logging` module alongside Loguru's `logger` object, and defines a single class to perform that connection [[target/app/core/logging.py]].

`InterceptHandler` is a custom `logging.Handler` subclass that acts as the bridge between the two systems [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. It declares no fields of its own beyond what it inherits from the standard handler base class [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. All of its logic lives in a single `emit` method, which receives a standard `logging.LogRecord` and translates it into a Loguru log call [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]].

The translation process has three steps. First, `emit` resolves the correct Loguru level name from `record.levelname`, falling back to the record's numeric level string if no matching named Loguru level exists [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. Second, to ensure Loguru attributes the log entry to the correct call site rather than to an internal frame inside the `logging` module, it walks the call stack upward from `logging.currentframe()`, incrementing a depth counter for every frame that still belongs to the standard `logging` machinery [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. Third, it calls `logger.opt` with the computed depth and the record's `exc_info` so that any exception context is preserved, then forwards the resolved level and the record's formatted message through that opt-configured logger [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]].

[`target/app/core/settings/app.py`](target/app/core/settings/app.py) is the runtime configuration module for the application, importing logging utilities, Pydantic types, and the `InterceptHandler` from the project's logging support before defining the single class that governs all live settings [[target/app/core/settings/app.py]].

The central definition is `AppSettings`, a Pydantic model that inherits from `BaseAppSettings` and holds every configurable value the application needs at runtime [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. Because `validate_assignment` is enabled, Pydantic re-validates any field value whenever it is reassigned after the object is first constructed [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. The fields are organised around four concerns: FastAPI application metadata (`debug`, `docs_url`, `openapi_prefix`, `openapi_url`, `redoc_url`, `title`, and `version`), database connectivity (`database_url` as a required `PostgresDsn`, `max_connection_count`, and `min_connection_count`), security (`secret_key` as a required `SecretStr`, `api_prefix`, `jwt_token_prefix`, and `allowed_hosts`), and logging (`logging_level` and the `loggers` tuple naming the two Uvicorn loggers) [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. The `app_env` field, typed as `AppEnvTypes` with a production default, is inherited from `BaseAppSettings` rather than declared directly in this class [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]].

`AppSettings` also exposes two methods that act on those fields. The `configure_logging` method wires the application's logging pipeline by replacing the root logger's handlers with a single `InterceptHandler`, attaching per-name `InterceptHandler` instances at `self.logging_level` to each logger listed in `self.loggers`, and registering a single `sys.stderr` sink through `logger.configure` [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. The `fastapi_kwargs` method assembles the FastAPI metadata fields into a plain dictionary so that it can be unpacked directly as keyword arguments when the FastAPI application instance is constructed [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. Together, the two methods mean that `AppSettings` is not merely a passive data container: it actively initialises both the logging subsystem and the web framework from the same source of truth [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]].

This module defines the typed table descriptors and query-parameter helper used to build SQL queries throughout the application [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py]].

The foundation is `TypedTable`, a subclass of pypika's `Table` that adds a declarative `__table__` class attribute for naming the underlying database table [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable]]. When instantiated, it resolves the table name by checking first for an explicit argument, then for `__table__`, and finally falling back to the class's own `__name__`, forwarding the result to pypika's `Table` constructor [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable]]. All other table descriptors in the module inherit from it.

`Users` maps to the `"users"` table and declares two fields, `id` (`int`) and `username` (`str`) [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Users]]. `Articles` maps to the `articles` table and carries eight fields — `id`, `slug`, `title`, `description`, `body`, `author_id`, `created_at`, and `updated_at` — covering both the article content and its authorship and timestamp metadata [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Articles]]. `Tags` is the simplest descriptor, representing the `tags` table with a single `tag` (`str`) field [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Tags]]. `ArticlesToTags` represents the join table that associates articles with tags, declaring `article_id` (`int`) and `tag` (`str`) [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::ArticlesToTags]]. `Favorites` maps to the `"favorites"` table and holds two integer foreign-key columns, `article_id` and `user_id`, linking articles to the users who have favourited them [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Favorites]].

Alongside the table descriptors, the module defines `Parameter`, a thin subclass of pypika's `CommonParameter` whose sole job is to emit asyncpg-style positional placeholders such as `$1` or `$2` when building dynamic queries [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Parameter]]. Its constructor accepts an integer `count` and immediately formats it into the string `"${count}"` before delegating to the parent class, keeping the rest of the query-building code free of placeholder-formatting details [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Parameter]].

Finally, the module instantiates one module-level singleton for each descriptor — `users`, `articles`, `tags`, `articles_to_tags`, and `favorites` — so that query-building code elsewhere can reference these shared table objects directly without constructing new instances [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py]].

[`target/app/db/repositories/articles.py`](target/app/db/repositories/articles.py) is the data-access module for all article-related database operations, and it establishes a small set of module-level constants used across the repository [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py]]. The string constants `AUTHOR_USERNAME_ALIAS` and `SLUG_ALIAS` name the column aliases expected in raw query results, while `CAMEL_OR_SNAKE_CASE_TO_WORDS` holds a regex pattern used for identifier parsing [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py]].

The module's single class, `ArticlesRepository`, is the data-access class responsible for all database operations relating to articles, inheriting from `BaseRepository` [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. Because it deliberately contains a higher-than-usual number of methods, it carries a `# noqa: WPS214` suppression [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. On construction, it creates two collaborating repositories — a `ProfilesRepository` and a `TagsRepository` — both sharing the same database connection, so article-level operations can delegate profile and tag lookups without opening separate connections [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].

Two private helpers underpin the public interface. `_get_article_from_db_record` assembles a fully populated `Article` domain object from a raw database row, accepting `slug` and `author_username` as separate parameters, fetching the author profile with follow-state awareness, retrieving associated tags and favorites count, and resolving the `favorited` flag only when a `requested_user` is present [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `_link_article_with_tags` associates a sequence of tag strings with an article by slug, writing one mapping per tag through the query layer [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].

The write operations form a coherent group. `create_article` persists a new article and its tags atomically inside a transaction before hydrating and returning a full domain object [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `update_article` deep-copies the existing article, overlays any supplied field replacements, and executes the update within a transaction keyed by the original slug and author [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `delete_article` removes the article row within a transaction using the same slug-and-author-username key [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].

The read operations cover both single-record and collection lookups. `get_article_by_slug` fetches and hydrates one article, raising `EntityDoesNotExist` when no matching row is found [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `filter_articles` builds a dynamic pypika query that can optionally join on tags, author, or favorites, and returns a paginated, personalised list of hydrated `Article` objects [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `get_articles_for_user_feed` queries for articles written by authors the requesting user follows and hydrates each raw row before returning the list [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].

The remaining methods handle tag and favorites data as discrete concerns. `get_tags_for_article_by_slug` returns all tags for an article as a flat list of strings, and `get_favorites_count_for_article_by_slug` returns the integer count of users who have favorited a given article [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `is_article_favorited_by_user` delegates to the query layer and returns the boolean result directly, while `add_article_into_favorites` and `remove_article_from_favorites` respectively persist and delete the favorite relationship between a user and an article [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].

[`target/app/db/repositories/base.py`](target/app/db/repositories/base.py) is a small foundational module that imports `Connection` from `asyncpg` and defines the single class `BaseRepository`, which acts as the shared base for all database repository classes in the project [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py]]. `BaseRepository` declares no parent classes of its own, keeping it a plain Python class [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]]. It accepts an asyncpg `Connection` instance at construction time and stores it in the private attribute `_conn`, making the active database connection available to every subclass that needs to run queries [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]]. A read-only `connection` property exposes `_conn` to those subclasses without requiring them to reference the private attribute directly, providing a clean and consistent interface to the underlying connection [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]].

This module is the data-access layer for comment persistence, importing the connection primitives, query catalogue, base repository infrastructure, and the domain models it needs to operate [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py]].

Its sole export is `CommentsRepository`, a class that extends `BaseRepository` and centralises every database operation involving comments [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]]. During initialisation the class sets up the database connection through the parent and also constructs a `ProfilesRepository` instance that it keeps as an internal collaborator, allowing it to resolve author profiles whenever it needs to materialise a full domain object [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]].

The private helper `_get_comment_from_db_record` is the single point where a raw database row is converted into a `Comment` domain object: it reads the scalar fields directly from the record and then calls out asynchronously to the embedded `ProfilesRepository` to attach the author's profile, ensuring that follow-relationship state is always reflected correctly from the perspective of the requesting user [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]]. Every public method that must return a `Comment` routes through this helper, giving the class a consistent hydration path [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]].

The four public methods cover the full lifecycle of a comment. `create_comment_for_article` inserts a new row and immediately hydrates it into a domain object so the caller receives a complete result in one asynchronous step [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]]. `get_comment_by_id` looks up a single comment by its numeric identifier and the parent article slug, raising `EntityDoesNotExist` if no matching row is found [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]]. `get_comments_for_article` retrieves every comment attached to an article by slug, mapping each row through the shared helper [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]]. Finally, `delete_comment` permanently removes the row corresponding to a given `Comment` object [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]].

The module [`target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py`](target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py) defines the data-access layer for user profiles and follower relationships within the application [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py]]. It introduces a `UserLike` type alias that accepts either a `User` or a `Profile` object, providing a flexible parameter type for the follow-management methods that follow [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py]].

The single class defined here, `ProfilesRepository`, is a database repository responsible for all profile and follower operations, inheriting its connection-management infrastructure from `BaseRepository` [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. At construction time it delegates to the parent via `super().__init__(conn)` and immediately creates an internal `UsersRepository` bound to the same connection, stored as `self._users_repo`, so that profile lookups can cross-reference user records without opening a second database connection [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]].

Four public async methods make up the repository's interface [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. `get_profile_by_username` retrieves a user through `self._users_repo` and assembles a `Profile` populated with `username`, `bio`, and `image`; when an optional `requested_user` argument is provided it additionally resolves the `following` field by calling `is_user_following_for_another_user` [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. `is_user_following_for_another_user` issues a database query with both users' usernames and returns the `"is_following"` boolean from the result, forming the shared primitive that `get_profile_by_username` depends on [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. `add_user_into_followers` wraps `queries.subscribe_user_to_another` in an atomic transaction to persist a follow relationship, accepting both participants as keyword-only `UserLike` arguments [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. `remove_user_from_followers` mirrors that operation by executing `queries.unsubscribe_user_from_another` inside a transaction to atomically delete the corresponding follow record [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]].

This module defines the data-access layer for tag records in the application [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py]]. It imports from the shared `queries` object and from `BaseRepository`, establishing the foundation for all database interaction [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py]].

The single class it exports, `TagsRepository`, extends `BaseRepository` and is responsible for managing tag records in the database [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]]. It exposes two asynchronous methods that together cover the two fundamental tag operations: writing new tags and reading all existing ones [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]].

The first method, `create_tags_that_dont_exist`, accepts a sequence of tag strings and persists any that are not yet stored, delegating to `queries.create_new_tags` and passing the repository's active connection along with the tags reshaped into a list of `{"tag": tag}` dicts [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository::create_tags_that_dont_exist]]. It returns nothing, making it a pure write operation [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository::create_tags_that_dont_exist]].

The second method, `get_all_tags`, retrieves every tag from the database by calling `queries.get_all_tags` with the repository's active connection, then flattens the result by extracting the first element of each row and returning the whole set as a `List[str]` [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository::get_all_tags]]. Together, these two methods give callers everything they need to keep the tag table consistent and to enumerate its full contents [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]].

The [`target/app/db/repositories/users.py`](target/app/db/repositories/users.py) module serves as the data-access layer for user records, providing all persistence operations — creation, lookup by email or username, and updates — through a single repository class [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py]]. It imports domain models `User` and `UserInDB`, the pre-compiled `queries` object, `BaseRepository` for connection management, and `EntityDoesNotExist` for signalling missing records [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py]].

The sole class defined here is `UsersRepository`, which inherits from `BaseRepository` and implements every database operation the application needs for user persistence [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]]. Creation is handled by `create_user`, which constructs a `UserInDB` in memory, hashes the password, executes an insert inside an explicit transaction via `queries.create_new_user`, and merges any database-generated values back onto the returned model so the caller always receives a fully populated record [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]]. Lookup is provided by two methods: `get_user_by_email` queries by email address and raises `EntityDoesNotExist` when no row matches, while `get_user_by_username` does the same keyed by username, both hydrating a successful result into a `UserInDB` instance [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]]. Finally, `update_user` ties the other methods together — it first fetches the current persisted state via `get_user_by_username`, selectively overwrites only the fields for which a new non-falsy value was supplied (`username`, `email`, `bio`, `image`), re-hashes the password through `change_password` when a new one is provided, and then flushes all changes inside a database transaction before returning the fully updated `UserInDB` to the caller [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]].

[`target/app/models/common.py`](target/app/models/common.py) is a shared Pydantic utilities module that provides two reusable mixin classes for domain models throughout the application [[target/app/models/common.py]]. It imports `datetime`, `pydantic.BaseModel`, `pydantic.Field`, and `pydantic.validator` to support the behaviour defined in those mixins [[target/app/models/common.py]].

`IDModelMixin` is a Pydantic `BaseModel` subclass whose sole responsibility is to supply a standard integer identity field to any model that inherits from it [[target/app/models/common.py::IDModelMixin]]. It declares a single field `id_` typed as `int` with a default of `0` and an alias of `"id"`, so that an external source such as a database row or JSON payload can supply the conventional `"id"` key while the Python attribute remains `id_` to avoid shadowing the built-in `id` function [[target/app/models/common.py::IDModelMixin]].

`DateTimeModelMixin` is a second Pydantic `BaseModel` subclass that mixes timestamp-tracking behaviour into other models [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]]. It declares two `datetime.datetime` fields, `created_at` and `updated_at`, both defaulting to `None` [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]]. A `pre` validator named `default_datetime` is attached to both fields and ensures they are always populated with a meaningful value: it returns the supplied value unchanged when it is truthy, and falls back to `datetime.datetime.now()` when the value is absent or falsy, so timestamps are set automatically at instantiation even if the caller omits them [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin::default_datetime]].

The two mixins are designed to be combined with one another and with application-specific models through multiple inheritance, giving any downstream model a consistent identity field and automatic timestamp population without repeating that logic in each model [[target/app/models/common.py::IDModelMixin]] [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]].

This module defines the domain-level user models used throughout the application [[target/app/models/domain/users.py]]. It imports shared mixins and the base `RWModel` from sibling packages, as well as the `security` service for password operations [[target/app/models/domain/users.py]].

The central type is `User`, a Pydantic model that represents an application user in memory [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::User]]. It inherits from `RWModel`, which supplies shared configuration such as automatic camelCase aliasing [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::User]]. The class carries four fields: `username` and `email` are required strings, `bio` is an optional string defaulting to an empty string, and `image` is an `Optional[str]` defaulting to `None` [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::User]].

`UserInDB` extends `User` to represent a user record as it exists in the database [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. It composes three base classes — `IDModelMixin`, `DateTimeModelMixin`, and `User` — gaining an integer primary-key field `id_` aliased to `"id"`, plus `created_at` and `updated_at` datetime fields, in addition to all four fields inherited from `User` [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. On top of those, `UserInDB` adds its own `salt` and `hashed_password` string fields, both defaulting to an empty string, which together store the credential material for the record [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]].

Two methods on `UserInDB` encapsulate all password logic. `change_password` mutates the instance in place by generating a fresh salt via `security.generate_salt`, storing it, then computing the hash of the salt-concatenated plain-text password via `security.get_password_hash` and writing the result into `hashed_password` [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. `check_password` verifies a supplied plain-text password by concatenating the stored salt with it and delegating to `security.verify_password` alongside the stored hash, returning `True` on a match and `False` otherwise [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. Together these two methods mean that no code outside this model needs to interact directly with the security service for user credential management [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]].

The `schemas` package is the API contract layer of the application, grouping all Pydantic models that validate incoming request data and shape outgoing response payloads [[target/app/models/schemas]]. Its [`__init__.py`](target/app/models/schemas/__init__.py) marks the directory as a Python package, making every submodule importable as part of the broader application [[target/app/models/schemas/__init__.py]].

The shared serialisation foundation is provided by [`rwschema.py`](target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py), which defines `RWSchema` — a thin subclass of `RWModel` that switches on `orm_mode = True`, allowing Pydantic to populate model instances directly from database rows rather than only from plain dictionaries [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]]. No new fields are added at this level; its sole job is to act as the bridge between the domain model layer and any schema class that must be constructed from persistence results [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]].

User-facing identity flows are covered by two submodules. [`users.py`](target/app/models/schemas/users.py) defines the full lifecycle of a user account: `UserInLogin` captures email and password for sign-in, `UserInCreate` extends that with a `username` field for registration, `UserWithToken` pairs domain profile fields with a session token for authenticated responses, `UserInResponse` wraps that combined object in a `user` envelope for API callers, and `UserInUpdate` exposes all five editable profile fields as optional so that any subset of changes constitutes a valid update payload [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInLogin]] [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInCreate]] [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserWithToken]] [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInUpdate]]. [`jwt.py`](target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py) sits alongside it, defining `JWTMeta` to carry token-level properties such as expiry and subject, and `JWTUser` to carry the application-level username extracted once a token has been decoded [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTMeta]] [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTUser]].

Article data is handled by [`articles.py`](target/app/models/schemas/articles.py), which establishes module-level pagination constants `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_LIMIT` (20) and `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_OFFSET` (0) and organises its schemas into request, response, and filter shapes [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py]]. `ArticleInCreate` collects the required title, description, and body plus an optional tag list, while `ArticleInUpdate` makes all three text fields optional for partial edits [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInCreate]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInUpdate]]. `ArticleForResponse` is the central response building block, combining domain article fields with a `tagList`-aliased tags field; `ArticleInResponse` wraps it in a single `article` envelope, and `ListOfArticlesInResponse` pairs a list of those objects with an `articles_count` integer for list endpoints [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleForResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ListOfArticlesInResponse]]. `ArticlesFilters`, which inherits from `BaseModel` directly rather than `RWSchema`, bundles the optional tag, author, and favorited filters with constrained limit and offset pagination fields for query-parameter handling [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticlesFilters]].

Comment operations are defined in [`comments.py`](target/app/models/schemas/comments.py), where `CommentInCreate` validates a single `body` string on input, `CommentInResponse` wraps a single `Comment` domain object for single-resource responses, and `ListOfCommentsInResponse` holds a list of `Comment` objects for collection responses, with all three classes inheriting from `RWSchema` [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInCreate]] [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::ListOfCommentsInResponse]].

Profile responses are handled by the compact [`profiles.py`](target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py) module, whose sole class `ProfileInResponse` wraps a `Profile` domain object under a `profile` key, with Pydantic managing all field validation and serialisation automatically [[target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py::ProfileInResponse]]. Finally, [`tags.py`](target/app/models/schemas/tags.py) provides `TagsInList`, a minimal `BaseModel` subclass that holds a `List[str]` of tag name strings, serving as the structured container whenever a collection of tags is transmitted as a validated payload [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py::TagsInList]].

The `services` package is the application's business-logic layer, acting as an intermediary between the API layer and the database and domain models [[target/app/services]]. Its presence as a Python namespace is established by an empty initialiser that makes the entire layer importable without contributing any definitions of its own [[target/app/services/__init__.py]].

Authentication-related credential checks live in [`authentication.py`](target/app/services/authentication.py), which exposes `check_email_is_taken` and `check_username_is_taken` — two functions that translate a repository-level `EntityDoesNotExist` exception into a plain boolean result, giving callers a clean availability check without needing to handle exceptions directly [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_email_is_taken]] [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken]].

Article-related service logic is handled by [`articles.py`](target/app/services/articles.py), which provides three focused helpers [[target/app/services/articles.py]]. `check_article_exists` performs a safe, boolean-returning guard by delegating to the repository and catching `EntityDoesNotExist` so callers never have to [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_article_exists]]. `check_user_can_modify_article` complements it by comparing the article's author username against the requesting user's username, returning `True` only when they match [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_user_can_modify_article]]. `get_slug_for_article` rounds out the module by delegating title-to-slug transformation to the `slugify` library, keeping slug generation consistent and centralised [[target/app/services/articles.py::get_slug_for_article]].

Comment authorisation follows the same ownership-check pattern in [`comments.py`](target/app/services/comments.py), where `check_user_can_modify_comment` accepts a `Comment` and a `User` and returns `True` only when the comment's author matches the given user [[target/app/services/comments.py::check_user_can_modify_comment]].

Token issuance and decoding are centralised in [`jwt.py`](target/app/services/jwt.py), which is built on the `HS256` algorithm with a fixed one-week expiry window [[target/app/services/jwt.py]]. The low-level `create_jwt_token` merges an arbitrary payload with expiry metadata and returns a signed JWT string [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_jwt_token]], while `create_access_token_for_user` wraps it with user-specific logic and an expiry window derived from `ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES` [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_access_token_for_user]]. The reverse direction is handled by `get_username_from_token`, which decodes a JWT and raises a descriptive `ValueError` for either a decode failure or a malformed payload [[target/app/services/jwt.py::get_username_from_token]].

Password security is concentrated in [`security.py`](target/app/services/security.py), which initialises a shared `passlib` `CryptContext` configured for bcrypt [[target/app/services/security.py]]. `generate_salt` produces a fresh random salt on each call [[target/app/services/security.py::generate_salt]], `get_password_hash` hashes a plain-text password via that shared context [[target/app/services/security.py::get_password_hash]], and `verify_password` compares a plain-text candidate against its stored hash, returning a boolean result — the two together forming a complementary pair for storing and later authenticating user credentials [[target/app/services/security.py::get_password_hash]] [[target/app/services/security.py::verify_password]].

The `dependencies` package groups all FastAPI dependency functions for the application's API layer into one importable namespace [[target/app/api/dependencies]]. Its [`__init__.py`](target/app/api/dependencies/__init__.py) is intentionally empty, acting only as a package marker and defining no symbols of its own [[target/app/api/dependencies/__init__.py]].

The foundation of the package is [`database.py`](target/app/api/dependencies/database.py), which establishes the three-level chain that every other module in the package relies on: it retrieves the application-level connection pool from `request.app.state.pool`, acquires a single connection from that pool for the lifetime of the request, and exposes a `get_repository` factory that instantiates any `BaseRepository` subclass bound to that connection [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py]].

Authentication is handled entirely by [`authentication.py`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py), which covers JWT Bearer token extraction, validation, and user resolution [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py]].
